title: How to Teach Secondary Students to Improve Their Penmanship (According to a Non-Expert) g-to-a-non-expert
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Dave Stuart Jr. shares a short, scripted mini-lesson he uses with ninth graders whose handwriting has become illegible, arguing that legibility is a learnable skill rather than a fixed trait. He walks through the exact classroom script he delivers, then distills it into four simple, repeatable principles: every act of handwriting is a rep, handwriting is a skill like any other, slowing down aids quality, and improvement can be targeted one letter at a time. The piece is a small, practical example of what Stuart elsewhere calls "Woodenizing" - taking a small but important behavior and teaching it explicitly rather than assuming students already know how to do it. It reflects his broader preference for paper-based work over screens because of its lower distraction cost and physical flexibility.
points: Frames handwriting as an improvable skill akin to an instrument or a sport, not a fixed trait, which lowers student defensiveness about correction.
Provides a fully scripted mini-lesson teachers can lift directly into their own classrooms, modeling how brief, explicit instruction beats vague reminders to "write neater."
The "pick one letter to improve" tactic narrows an overwhelming goal (better handwriting) into a single, trackable unit of practice.
Frames the exercise as a case of "Woodenizing" - leaving nothing to chance when teaching a small but consequential behavior.
quotes: Whenever I can have my students do work on paper, I do. Paper is less wrought with temptation than a Chrome tab is; it requires no battery charge; you can move it around between people and places without copying a link or clicking a button.

The trouble with having students write things by hand, however, is that there are always at least a handful amongst my ninth graders who have significant struggles with writing legibly. As in, what they transcribe may as well be cuneiform.
Think of handwriting like a learnable skill, such as playing an instrument or throwing a ball; some of you aren't so good at playing an instrument
Lots of times if you just think, "I'm going to write a bit more slowly and carefully right now," you'll be able to focus on your skill and improve it a bit.
Pick just one letter in the way that they handwrite. Draw it as carefully as you can someplace that you'll see it frequently
These basic things will make you a better handwriter - not a handtyper, but a handwriter. And that's all that we're after with this little mini-lesson.
